name: Naba
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Scherrer, Elaine Marie. 2022. A phonological description of Naba. Afrika und Übersee 95: 76-134. Hamburg University Press. DOI 10.15460/auue.2022.95.1.255 (open access, peer-reviewed article).
catalog_locator: Section 4 'Tone', p. 95, and section 4.1 'Tone-bearing units', p. 95; section 4.2 'Tone melodies' with footnote 8, p. 97
catalog_quote: Naba is a tonal language, with three level tones, High (H), Mid (M) and Low (L). The majority of words, especially nouns and verbs, have an underlying tone melody which consists either of one level tone or a sequence of levels. However, a good number of grammatical function morphemes, such as clitics, particles, and verbal affixes, are underlyingly toneless. The analysis of Naba's tonal system is ongoing, so this section will be only a brief overview of what has been discovered so far. [p. 95] ... Many words are distinguished solely by tone melody as in the examples presented in (19) ... From the examples in the right column it is shown that in Naba tone attaches to moras rather than to syllables. VV sequences that form a single syllable can carry two different tones. [p. 95] ... Naba has nine attested tone melodies, with two (MH and LHL) being rare enough to question their validity. The melodies manifest themselves differently depending on the number of moras in the word to which they apply. [p. 96] ... Among level tone melodies, M is the most common, with HL being by far the most common melody overall, particularly among verbs. [p. 97] ... 8 LHL is almost exclusively found in Chadian Arabic loan words, reflecting the stress system of that language. [fn. 8, p. 97]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given: the only phonological description that could be opened treats Naba as a three-level tone language (H, M, L on moras; nine lexical melodies, M commonest, HL commonest overall; toneless clitics/affixes) and never mentions word stress or accent in Naba. The one use of 'stress' (fn. 8) refers to the stress system of Chadian Arabic as the origin of an LHL melody in loanwords.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: MH and LHL melodies are rare, LHL confined to Chadian Arabic loans; HH sequences restricted; downstep and tone spreading described (4.4).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone melodies on nouns and verbs; analysis based on citation forms and short phrases (plural =ge clitic used to reveal underlying melodies); author states the tone analysis is 'incomplete' and grammatical tone still under study (p. 78). Describes the Yao sub-dialect of Bilala.
new_statements.identity_note: Scherrer 2022 treats Naba (= Bilala/Kuka/Medogo; community name 'Melbene') as a single language (citing Maass 2001) and describes the Yao sub-dialect of the Bilala dialect (main informant from Yao; p. 77-78). Glottolog naba1253 has no separate dialect codes listed on the downloaded page; the Bilala sub-dialects (Yao, Ambassatna, Amjamena-bilala, Moeto) are speaker-acknowledged only. The earlier scan's 'no source found' classification was wrong: Glottolog 5.1 lists Scherrer 2022 (listed by Glottolog as a phonology) and it is open access.

sources.note: Full segmental + tonal phonology (sections 2-6). Section 4 'Tone' (p. 95) states Naba is a tonal language with three level tones H, M, L attaching to moras; nine tone melodies; toneless grammatical morphemes. There is no stress/accent/prominence section and no statement about word stress in Naba anywhere in the 60 pages; the single occurrence of 'stress' is footnote 8 (p. 97), which attributes the rare LHL melody of Chadian Arabic loanwords to 'the stress system of that language' (Arabic), not to Naba. Dialect described: Yao sub-dialect of Bilala (p. 77-78).

tone.quote: Le système *OCC, commun à ces dernières et notamment caractérisé par le développement d'un troisième registre tonal, se subdivise à son tour en cinq rameaux ... les parlers septentrionaux (bulala, beraku, kenga, 'barma) occupant une situation indécise ou ambivalente.
tone.locator: (Boyeldieu 2006 'Presentation des langues SBB'), section 'Classification, genealogie et histoire des langues': first fragment in the paragraph giving the genealogical schema after 'Boyeldieu (2000) a propose une classification historique, fondee sur la comparaison tonale'; second fragment ('les parlers septentrionaux (bulala, beraku, kenga, 'barma) occupant une situation indecise ou ambivalente') about 1,300 characters later at the end of the next paragraph; the ellipsis skips the intervening text. Both fragments verbatim.
tone.translation: The *OCC system, common to the latter [the 'western' languages] and characterised notably by the development of a third tonal register, subdivides in turn into five branches ... the northern lects (Bulala, Beraku, Kenga, 'Barma) occupying an undecided or ambivalent position.
